# Regular expressions with `std/re`

Comparing strings with `==` only works when they are exactly the same. Once the rule gets fuzzy, for
example "pull the name and the age out of one line", a chain of `split` and `strip` piles up and
becomes hard to read. A regular expression writes that rule once, as a single pattern. Nim ships the
pattern engine in its standard library, in the `std/re` module.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write a pattern with `re"..."`, use `match`, `find`, and `findAll`,
replace and split text with `replace`, `replacef`, and `split`, read capture groups, turn on `(?i)`,
and tell when a regular expression is overkill because `strutils` is enough.
:::

## One pattern, two groups

`re"..."` turns the pattern text into a `Regex` value. The shortest form uses the `=~` template,
which fills a `matches` array with the capture groups. Save it as `main.nim`, then run
`nim c -r main.nim`.

```{.nim}
import std/re

let line = "Ada, 36"

# =~ declares a `matches` array that holds the capture groups.
if line =~ re"(\w+),\s*(\d+)":
  echo "name: ", matches[0]
  echo "age: ", matches[1]
else:
  echo "no match"
```

```{.txt}
name: Ada
age: 36
```

`matches[0]` is not the whole match; it is the first group, the contents of the first pair of
parentheses. The second group lands in `matches[1]`. Nim keeps no separate slot for the whole match
in this array; when you need that value, wrap the entire pattern in parentheses.

The pattern symbols you will use most: `\w` matches one letter or digit, `\d` matches one digit,
and `\s` matches one space. Adding `+` means "one time or more", so `\w+` swallows a whole word.

## `match` is anchored, `find` scans

These two procedures are easy to mix up. `match` tests the pattern from the start of the string, as
if nailed to position zero. `find` scans the whole string and returns the index of the first match,
or `-1` when there is none.

```{.nim}
import std/re

let text = "Ada Lovelace, 36"

# match is anchored at the start of the string; find scans the whole string.
echo "match from start: ", text.match(re"Ada")
echo "match in the middle: ", text.match(re"Lovelace")
echo "find in the middle: ", text.find(re"Lovelace")

# The openArray overload fills the capture groups and returns the start index.
var captures: array[2, string]
if text.find(re"(\w+),\s*(\d+)", captures) >= 0:
  echo "name: ", captures[0]
  echo "age: ", captures[1]
```

```{.txt}
match from start: true
match in the middle: false
find in the middle: 4
name: Lovelace
age: 36
```

To collect the capture groups as well, allocate the array first, then hand it to the `find` variant
that takes an `openArray[string]`. That version returns the index and fills the array; `-1` means no
match, so the result is tested with `>= 0`.

## Every match with `findAll`

`findAll` gathers every matching piece. It has two forms: an iterator that yields one match per
turn, and a procedure that returns a `seq[string]`. Using it directly inside `echo` picks the
second form.

```{.nim}
import std/re

let log = "2024-03-01 INFO ok 2024-03-02 WARN slow"

echo "dates: ", log.findAll(re"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}")
echo "levels: ", log.findAll(re"\b[A-Z]{4}\b")

for word in log.findAll(re"[a-z]+"):
  echo "word: ", word
```

```{.txt}
dates: @["2024-03-01", "2024-03-02"]
levels: @["INFO", "WARN"]
word: ok
word: slow
```

The `\b` marker stands for a word boundary, so `\b[A-Z]{4}\b` matches only a four-letter uppercase
word that stands on its own. Braces set an exact repetition count.

One trap: an empty pattern such as `re"a*"` matches the empty string anywhere. The `findAll`
iterator deliberately stops on an empty match so the loop does not run forever.

## Replacing and splitting

`replace` swaps every match for new text. To put capture groups back in, use `replacef` with `$1`,
`$2`, and so on. `split` cuts the string on every match and returns a sequence of the pieces.

```{.nim}
import std/re

let raw = "  Ada   Lovelace  "

echo "[", raw.replace(re"\s+", " "), "]"
echo "[", raw.replace(re"^\s+|\s+$", ""), "]"

let phone = "0812-3456-7890"
echo phone.replace(re"\D", "")

# replacef understands $1, $2, ... for the capture groups.
let name = "Ada Lovelace"
echo name.replacef(re"(\w+)\s+(\w+)", "$2, $1")

# split cuts the string on every match of the pattern.
let record = "ada, 36,london"
echo record.split(re",\s*")
```

```{.txt}
[ Ada Lovelace ]
[Ada   Lovelace]
081234567890
Lovelace, Ada
@["ada", "36", "london"]
```

The pattern `^\s+|\s+$` holds two rules separated by `|`: one anchored at the start, one at the end.
Because `replace` swaps every match, both are cut in one call, while the spaces inside the sentence
stay untouched. The marker `\D` is the opposite of `\d`: anything that is not a digit.

## Flags and escaped characters

A small flag such as `(?i)` goes at the start of the pattern and applies until the end. To make one
character count as a plain letter, put a `\` in front of it.

```{.nim}
import std/re
import std/strutils

# (?i) makes the rest of the pattern case-insensitive.
echo "NIM".match(re"(?i)nim")
echo "NIM".match(re"nim")

# re"..." is a raw string: write one backslash, not two.
echo "a.b".match(re"a\.b")
echo "axb".match(re"a\.b")

# For a fixed prefix or suffix, strutils is shorter than a regex.
echo "report.txt".endsWith(".txt")
```

```{.txt}
true
false
true
false
true
```

`re"..."` is a raw string, so a backslash is written once. A plain string needs two, `"\\d"`, to
produce the same backslash. Without `\`, the dot character means "any letter", so `a.b` also matches
`axb`.

## Intentional error: forgetting to import `std/re`

The names from `std/re` do not appear out of nowhere. Drop the `import`, and the compiler stops at
the first token.

```{.nim}
let pattern = re"(\d+)"
echo "abc 12".findAll(pattern)
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(1, 15) Error: undeclared identifier: 're'
```

Read it from the left: file, position `(line, column)`, severity, then the message. The position
`(1, 15)` is the start of `re` in `re"(\d+)"`. `undeclared identifier` means the name is used
without ever being imported. The shortest fix: add `import std/re` on the first line.

One thing worth knowing: `re` processes the pattern at runtime. A pattern with a typo, say an
unclosed parenthesis, raises an exception only when the program runs, not at compile time.

## When a regular expression is overkill

A regular expression quickly turns into text nobody else can read. For fixed prefixes and suffixes,
`strutils` is shorter. The example above uses `endsWith(".txt")`, not a pattern.

- Use `strutils` when you look for one literal piece: `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `contains`.
- Use a regular expression when the shape repeats, branches, or needs capture groups.
- Break a long pattern into named pieces; do not let one line hold all of it.

A regular expression is not a parser either. For nested structure such as JSON or HTML, use a module
that actually understands it, such as `std/json`.

## Exercises

1. Change the first example so the pattern also captures the city in `Ada, 36, London`, then print
   that city.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/re

   for m in "one1two22three333".findAll(re"\d+"):
     echo m
   ```
3. Write from scratch: a procedure that takes a `seq[string]` of email addresses and returns a
   `seq[string]` of the domain names, that is, the part after `@`.
4. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain its message:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/re

   if "Ada, 36" =~ re"(\w+), (\d+)":
     echo matches[0]

   echo matches[1]
   ```
5. Name one text task that `strutils` handles better than a regular expression.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `re"..."` turns text into a `Regex`; the `=~` template fills a `matches` array with the capture
  groups.
- `match` is anchored at the start of the string, `find` scans the whole string and returns an
  index.
- `findAll` collects every match; `replace`, `replacef`, and `split` change and split text.
- `(?i)` turns on case-insensitive matching; `re"..."` is a raw string.
- Patterns are processed at runtime, so a bad pattern shows up only when the program runs.
